newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco tax provision targeted by White House.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco tax provision targeted by White House.

text.p: Clinton administration officials said on Friday the value of any settlement with the tobacco industry may have to be increased to reflect a concession to the industry in new tax-cut legislation.
They said the industry did not act in good faith in winning passage of the provision in tax-cut legislation passed by Congress on Thursday and sent to U.S. President Bill Clinton.

The provision would give the tobacco industry credit for a 15-cent per pack increase in the cigarette tax, also passed in the bill. The credit would be applied to any settlement to resolve state and class-action lawsuits against the industry.

The overall cost to be paid by tobacco companies in the proposed settlement is now pegged at $368 billion over 25 years -- although Clinton has yet to agree to the deal. The current federal cigarette tax is 24 cents per pack.

"If the provision in the tax bill remains and we come to the conclusion that $368 (billion) was the right number to start with, then, sure, we'd add the 15 cents on top of that," said White House Domestic Policy Advisor Bruce Reed, co-leader of an admistration task force on the tobacco settlement.

"The 15 cents that we won for children's health this week will be on top of any settlement," Reed told reporters at the after meetings with tobacco retailers, advertisers and public health representatives.
"They (the tobacco industry) knew going into this that they were going to have to pay a tax on top of any settlement, and that's our position," he said.
Money from the cigarette tax increase is intended to help cover children with no health insurance.
Health and Human Services Secretary Donna Shalala said inclusion of the break for tobacco companies in the tax bill was a violation of good faith by the industry.

"In my judgment the tobacco companies did not indicate good faith in what they did on the tax side of the bill and that is something that we will remember as we advise the president, advise Congress as to what our position is," Shalala said.
"If they wanted to send us a message that they haven't changed their stripes, they certainly did that," she said.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said earlier on Friday that "our view is that the net liability that the companies will face as a result of the settlement is not likely going to be reduced by this provision."
McCurry said he did not believe the provision would be subject to new line-item veto authority granted to Clinton over certain tax and spending measures.

Congress after its August recess is expected to begin hearings on the proposed tobacco settlement, which would settle 40 state lawsuits and a slew of class actions against the industry. The settlement would have to be enacted by Congress and signed by Clinton to take effect.
